title: Design Browser History
description:
# Design Browser History

You have a browser with one tab. It starts at `homepage`, can visit a new URL, can move back through previous pages, and can move forward through pages that were left behind by back operations.

Implement the `BrowserHistory` class:

* `BrowserHistory(String homepage)` initializes the browser at `homepage`.
* `void visit(String url)` visits `url` from the current page. This clears all forward history that was ahead of the current page.
* `String back(int steps)` moves back by at most `steps` pages. If fewer pages exist behind the current page, stop at the earliest page. Return the current URL after moving.
* `String forward(int steps)` moves forward by at most `steps` pages. If fewer pages exist ahead of the current page, stop at the latest reachable page. Return the current URL after moving.

A visit creates a new history entry even if the URL text is the same as the current URL. Only the forward suffix is removed; pages behind the current page stay reachable.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1

**Input:**
["BrowserHistory","visit","visit","visit","back","back","forward","visit","forward","back","back"]
[["leetcode.com"],["google.com"],["facebook.com"],["youtube.com"],[1],[1],[1],["linkedin.com"],[2],[2],[7]]

**Output:**
[null,null,null,null,"facebook.com","google.com","facebook.com",null,"linkedin.com","google.com","leetcode.com"]

## Constraints

* `1 <= homepage.length <= 20`
* `1 <= url.length <= 20`
* `1 <= steps <= 100`
* `homepage` and `url` contain only `.` and lowercase English letters.
* At most `5000` calls are made to `visit`, `back`, and `forward`.

solutions.name: ArrayList with Logical Tail
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store pages in an `ArrayList`, track the current index, and track the last valid index. A visit advances the current index, writes the new page, and makes that index the new tail; old entries beyond the tail are ignored.

## Key Insight

Clearing forward history does not require physically deleting every stale page. A logical tail is enough as long as `forward` clamps against that tail instead of the list's physical size.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) for visit, back, and forward
- Space Complexity: O(n) for the stored pages

solutions.name: Fixed Array Active Window
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the operation limit to allocate one string array for all possible pages. Keep `index` as the current position and `size` as the active history length. Visiting writes at `index + 1` and shrinks `size` to discard forward entries.

## Key Insight

The browser history is a mutable prefix of an array. `size` is the contract boundary; anything after it is stale and must not be reachable by `forward`.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) for every operation
- Space Complexity: O(5000), which is O(n) under the call limit

solutions.name: Doubly Linked Node Chain
solutions.timeComplexity: O(steps) per back/forward, O(1) per visit
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent each page as a node with `prev` and `next` links, and keep a pointer to the current node. A visit creates a new node after current and drops the old `next` chain. Back and forward walk links until they run out or consume the requested steps.

## Key Insight

In a linked model, clearing forward history is exactly setting `current.next` to the newly visited page. No stale node remains reachable from the current timeline.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) for visit and O(steps) for back/forward
- Space Complexity: O(n) for reachable history nodes

solutions.name: Back and Forward Stacks
solutions.timeComplexity: O(steps) per back/forward, O(1) per visit
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep the current page separately, pages behind it in a back stack, and pages ahead of it in a forward stack. `back` transfers current pages to the forward stack; `forward` transfers them back; `visit` clears the forward stack.

## Key Insight

This mirrors the user mental model: after moving back, the pages you left become forward history, and visiting a new page throws that forward stack away.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) for visit and O(steps) for back/forward
- Space Complexity: O(n) for both stacks together

solutions.name: Cursor Array Linked Nodes
solutions.timeComplexity: O(steps) per back/forward, O(1) per visit
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store linked-list nodes in parallel arrays: `urls[id]`, `prev[id]`, and `next[id]`. The current page is an integer cursor. Visiting allocates a fresh id, links it after the current cursor, and overwrites the current cursor's `next` pointer.

## Key Insight

A linked list does not require object nodes. Cursor arrays make the pointer rewiring explicit and also show why stale forward nodes disappear once their incoming link is replaced.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) visit and O(steps) navigation
- Space Complexity: O(5000), bounded by the number of calls

tests.description: Back and forward clamp at the ends, and visit truncates forward history.
A one-page history cannot move until a visit creates another entry.
Visiting after a back operation clears every page that used to be ahead.
Exact boundary steps land on the first or last reachable page without overshooting.
Repeated visits to the same URL are still separate history entries.
The maximum step value clamps cleanly across a longer history.
A visit from the middle after moving forward must keep only the prefix ending at current.
Forward history must be cleared every time visit is called, even after alternating moves.
